Predicting the full-load electrical power output of a combined cycle power plant¶

Dataset: Combined Cycle Power Plant, UCI Machine Learning Repository (Tüfekci and Kaya), 9,568 hourly records. Models: support vector regression (RBF kernel), k-nearest neighbours regression, multilayer perceptron.

How to run¶

  1. Open the notebook in Google Colab and choose Runtime > Run all.
  2. When the upload box appears, upload Folds5x2_pp.xlsx (the original file from UCI). raw_data.csv also works.
  3. Every result, figure and exported file is produced by the cells below. All random processes use a fixed seed, so a second run gives the same numbers.
  4. A full run takes about 10 minutes on an 8-core laptop. Free Colab has 2 cores, so expect it to take longer there. Most of the time is spent tuning the SVR (section 7) and the MLP (section 9).

Files written by the notebook go to the outputs/ folder. In Colab, download them from the Files panel on the left.

1. Project setup and raw data¶

This section loads the libraries, fixes the random seed, finds the dataset and saves an unchanged copy of the raw data as raw_data.csv. The original raw data is kept unchanged, so this copy is never edited. All cleaning in section 4 works on a separate dataframe.

1.3 Load the raw data¶

The UCI Excel file has five sheets. They hold the same 9,568 rows in five different shuffled orders, which the original authors used for 5x2 cross-validation. Section 3 checks this claim. Sheet1 is used here as the raw dataset.

Columns, as defined by the dataset authors:

  • AT: ambient temperature, °C
  • V: exhaust vacuum, cm Hg
  • AP: ambient pressure, mbar
  • RH: relative humidity, %
  • PE: net electrical power output, hourly average, MW (the target)

2. Engineering problem formulation¶

2.1 The plant¶

A combined cycle power plant (CCPP) burns fuel once and produces electricity twice:

  1. Gas turbine (Brayton cycle). The compressor draws in outside air, the combustor burns fuel in it, and the hot gas expands through the turbine, which drives a generator.
  2. Heat recovery steam generator (HRSG). The gas turbine exhaust is still at roughly 500 to 600 °C. The HRSG uses this heat to boil water into high-pressure steam.
  3. Steam turbine (Rankine cycle). The steam expands through a second turbine, which drives another generator, and then condenses in the condenser so the water can be pumped back to the HRSG.

The plant in this dataset ran at full load for all 9,568 hours, so the operators were not changing the set point. The output still moved over a range of about 76 MW. With the throttle fixed, that variation comes from the conditions the plant cannot control: the state of the air entering the compressor and the pressure in the condenser. Those are the four measured inputs.

2.2 Inputs and target¶

The variable definitions and units come from the dataset authors. The ranges below are computed from the raw data. The last column is the direction of effect that thermodynamics predicts, before looking at any model. Section 12 checks the trained model against these signs.

In [6]:

    {
        "name": ["Ambient temperature", "Exhaust vacuum", "Ambient pressure",
                 "Relative humidity", "Net electrical output"],
        "unit": ["°C", "cm Hg", "mbar", "%", "MW"],
        "role": ["input", "input", "input", "input", "target"],
        "acts on": ["gas turbine (inlet air)", "steam turbine (back pressure)",
                    "gas turbine (inlet air)", "gas turbine (inlet air)", "whole plant"],
        "expected effect on PE": ["strong decrease", "decrease", "small increase",
                                  "small, uncertain sign", "n/a"],
    },
    index=EXPECTED_COLUMNS,
)
stats = raw.agg(["min", "max", "mean", "std"]).T
variables = variables.join(stats.round(2))
variables
Out[6]:
name unit role acts on expected effect on PE min max mean std
AT Ambient temperature °C input gas turbine (inlet air) strong decrease 1.81 37.11 19.65 7.45
V Exhaust vacuum cm Hg input steam turbine (back pressure) decrease 25.36 81.56 54.31 12.71
AP Ambient pressure mbar input gas turbine (inlet air) small increase 992.89 1033.30 1013.26 5.94
RH Relative humidity % input gas turbine (inlet air) small, uncertain sign 25.56 100.16 73.31 14.60
PE Net electrical output MW target whole plant n/a 420.26 495.76 454.37 17.07

Physical role of each input:

  • AT, ambient temperature. The compressor moves a roughly fixed volume of air per second. By the ideal gas law the air density is $\rho = p / (R\,T)$, so warmer air means less mass of air per second, less fuel can be burned at the same turbine inlet temperature, and the gas turbine produces less power. Warm air also raises the compressor work per kilogram. AT is expected to be the strongest input.
  • AP, ambient pressure. Higher pressure gives denser air and more mass flow through the compressor, so output should rise slightly. Over the observed range (about 4%) the effect is small.
  • RH, relative humidity. Water vapour (molar mass 18 g/mol) is lighter than dry air (29 g/mol), so humid air is slightly less dense. Vapour also has a higher specific heat, which changes the turbine work per kilogram. The net effect is small and its sign is not obvious in advance, which makes RH a useful test of what the models learn.
  • V, exhaust vacuum. V is measured at the steam turbine exhaust, on the condenser side. A lower condenser pressure lets the steam expand further, so the steam turbine extracts more enthalpy. In this dataset higher V goes with lower output, so a higher V reading corresponds to a higher back pressure. Note that the maximum V (81.6 cm Hg) is above atmospheric pressure (about 76 cm Hg), so V cannot be a literal vacuum gauge reading in cm Hg. Section 3 records this as a unit issue; the models only need V to be a consistent indicator of back pressure.
  • PE, net electrical output. The target. The UCI page calls it "net hourly electrical energy output", which describes an hourly average power, so the unit is MW. The reference paper (Santarisi and Faouri, 2021) labels it kWh, which does not fit values of 420 to 496.

AT and V are physically linked: on hot days the cooling water or air reaching the condenser is also warmer, so the condenser pressure rises. The two inputs are therefore correlated, and section 12 has to separate their effects with care.

The quick check below compares the coldest 5% of hours with the hottest 5%. It sets the ideal-gas density change of the inlet air against the observed change in output. It uses raw data, so it is an order-of-magnitude check, not a model.

In [7]:
cold = raw[raw["AT"] <= raw["AT"].quantile(0.05)]     # coldest 5% of hours
hot = raw[raw["AT"] >= raw["AT"].quantile(0.95)]      # hottest 5% of hours

# ideal gas: rho = p / (R T), so the density ratio needs mean T in kelvin and mean p
rho_ratio = (hot["AP"].mean() / (hot["AT"].mean() + 273.15)) / (
    cold["AP"].mean() / (cold["AT"].mean() + 273.15))
density_drop = 1 - rho_ratio
pe_drop = 1 - hot["PE"].mean() / cold["PE"].mean()

summary = pd.DataFrame({"coldest 5%": cold.mean(), "hottest 5%": hot.mean()}).T
display(summary.round(1))
print(f"Inlet air density drop, cold to hot (ideal gas, AT and AP): {density_drop:.1%}")
print(f"Observed drop in PE, cold to hot:                          {pe_drop:.1%}")
print(f"Share of the PE drop matched by the density drop:          {density_drop / pe_drop:.0%}")
AT V AP RH PE
coldest 5% 6.0 40.0 1016.7 84.3 485.2
hottest 5% 32.2 70.8 1008.3 51.9 432.7 
Inlet air density drop, cold to hot (ideal gas, AT and AP): 9.3%
Observed drop in PE, cold to hot:                          10.8%
Share of the PE drop matched by the density drop:          86%

The loss of inlet air density alone matches most of the drop in output. The remainder is consistent with the other effects of hot weather: higher compressor work per kilogram, and a warmer condenser (mean V rises from about 40 to 71 cm Hg between the two groups) that reduces steam turbine output. The inputs are physically sufficient to explain the target, which supports a data-driven model built on them.

2.3 Type of machine learning task¶

  • The target PE is a continuous quantity in MW, so this is supervised regression.
  • Classification would throw information away (for example "high" or "low" output) and is not what a grid operator needs.
  • The rows carry no timestamps and are not in time order (the five sheets are shuffled copies), so the data cannot be treated as a time series. Each row is an independent hourly snapshot of the plant at full load, and a randomized train/test split is justified (section 6).
  • The four inputs are measured at the same time as PE and none of them is calculated from PE, so none of them leaks the target.

2.4 Engineering decisions the model supports¶

  1. Committing output to the grid. A base-load plant tells the grid operator in advance how many MW it will deliver. Over-predicting means promising energy the plant cannot produce: the shortfall has to be covered by other plants and is usually penalized. Under-predicting leaves sellable capacity unused. Either error costs money, and over-prediction also affects grid balance.
  2. Performance monitoring. At full load, the model gives the output a healthy plant should produce under the current conditions. If the measured PE stays below the prediction for many hours, the gap points to degradation such as compressor fouling, turbine blade wear or condenser fouling. Here the model is an expected-performance baseline for condition monitoring.

These two uses lead to different input requirements. For performance monitoring all four inputs are measured live by plant sensors, so the full model applies. For a day-ahead grid commitment AT, AP and RH can come from a weather forecast, but V is a plant-side reading that is not known in advance. Section 10 therefore also reports how much accuracy is lost when V is left out.

2.5 Success criteria¶

The project is judged against measurable targets set before training any model:

  1. Accuracy on unseen data. On the held-out test set, MAPE below 1% (about 4.5 MW at the mean output), and better than the best result in the reference paper (gradient boosting, R² = 0.912, MAPE = 0.872%).
  2. Better than a trivial baseline. A model that always predicts the mean output has an RMSE equal to the standard deviation of PE (computed below). Every model must be far below this. The baseline MAPE is only about 3%, because PE varies by a modest share of its mean, so MAPE alone makes weak models look good. RMSE and R² are reported next to it.
  3. Generalization. Small gap between training and cross-validation error, and small spread of error across folds.
  4. Physical plausibility. The learned trends must match section 2.2: PE falls with AT and V and rises with AP. A model that scores well but breaks these trends is rejected.
  5. Practical cost. Training and prediction time, and how easily the result can be explained to plant engineers, are part of the final choice in section 10.
In [8]:
baseline_rmse = raw["PE"].std(ddof=0)
print(f"Mean-predictor baseline: RMSE = {baseline_rmse:.2f} MW, "
      f"MAPE = {np.mean(np.abs(raw['PE'] - raw['PE'].mean()) / raw['PE']):.2%}")

Mean-predictor baseline: RMSE = 17.07 MW, MAPE = 3.26%

2.6 Assumptions and scope¶

  • The model applies to this plant at full load only. Part-load operation, start-ups and shutdowns are not in the data.
  • Inputs are hourly averages, so the model predicts hourly average output, not second-by-second transients.
  • Predictions are reliable only inside the observed input ranges (section 2.2). A day hotter than 37 °C, for example, is an extrapolation.
  • The dataset does not record plant maintenance or degradation over the six years. Any slow drift in plant condition appears in the data as unexplained error.

3. Data audit¶

The audit runs on the raw data and changes nothing. The checks cover data types, duplicates, missing values, outliers, units, categorical variables, imbalance and leakage. Every finding is collected in a log, and section 4 decides what to do about each one.

audit_log = []          # one row per check: what was checked, what was found, what section 4 will do


def log(check, finding, action):
    audit_log.append({"check": check, "finding": finding, "planned action": action})

All five columns are numeric floats recorded to two decimal places. There are no text or categorical columns, so no encoding is needed. There is no timestamp or ID column either.

V has far fewer distinct values (634) than the other inputs. It looks like the condenser reading was logged at a coarser resolution than the ambient sensors. This does not stop it being used as a continuous input, but it limits how finely the models can resolve the effect of V.

3.3 The five sheets of the Excel file¶

The UCI page states that the five sheets are the same data shuffled five times. If that were wrong (for example, if each sheet held different hours), using only Sheet1 would throw data away. The check sorts each sheet and compares it with Sheet1.

In [12]:
if xlsx_path is not None:
    sheets = pd.read_excel(xlsx_path, sheet_name=None)


    def sort_rows(df):
        return df.sort_values(EXPECTED_COLUMNS).reset_index(drop=True)


    reference = sort_rows(sheets["Sheet1"])
    for name, sheet in sheets.items():
        same_rows = sort_rows(sheet).equals(reference)
        same_order = sheet.reset_index(drop=True).equals(sheets["Sheet1"])
        print(f"{name}: {sheet.shape[0]:,} rows, same rows as Sheet1: {same_rows}, same order: {same_order}")

    log("Five Excel sheets", "identical sets of rows in different orders",
        "use Sheet1 only; stacking sheets would copy every row five times")
else:
    print("Excel file not available, sheet check skipped (raw_data.csv already holds Sheet1).")

Sheet1: 9,568 rows, same rows as Sheet1: True, same order: True
Sheet2: 9,568 rows, same rows as Sheet1: True, same order: False
Sheet3: 9,568 rows, same rows as Sheet1: True, same order: False
Sheet4: 9,568 rows, same rows as Sheet1: True, same order: False
Sheet5: 9,568 rows, same rows as Sheet1: True, same order: False

All five sheets hold exactly the same rows in different orders. Only one sheet is used. Combining the sheets would repeat every record five times, and after a random split the same hour would sit in both the training and the test set. That would be severe leakage.

3.4 Duplicate records¶

In [13]:
FEATURES = ["AT", "V", "AP", "RH"]
TARGET = "PE"

n_dup = raw.duplicated().sum()
dup_rows = raw[raw.duplicated(keep=False)].sort_values(EXPECTED_COLUMNS)

# rows with identical inputs but different outputs would point to measurement noise or a hidden variable
input_groups = raw.groupby(FEATURES)[TARGET].nunique()
conflicting = (input_groups > 1).sum()

print(f"Exact duplicate rows (all five values equal): {n_dup} ({n_dup / len(raw):.2%})")
print(f"Rows involved (originals + copies):           {len(dup_rows)}")
print(f"Input combinations with more than one PE:     {conflicting}")
dup_rows.head(6)

Exact duplicate rows (all five values equal): 41 (0.43%)
Rows involved (originals + copies):           82
Input combinations with more than one PE:     0
Out[13]:
AT V AP RH PE
5045 6.03 41.17 1019.81 84.20 488.57
5320 6.03 41.17 1019.81 84.20 488.57
1186 6.06 41.17 1019.67 84.70 489.62
6008 6.06 41.17 1019.67 84.70 489.62
4261 6.40 41.17 1019.54 85.37 488.82
6131 6.40 41.17 1019.54 85.37 488.82

There are 41 exact duplicates: each one matches another row in all five columns to 0.01, and each appears exactly twice. No input combination appears with two different outputs.

Are they real repeated hours or copying errors? A genuine repeat would need two different hours to agree on temperature, vacuum, pressure, humidity and output, all to two decimal places. RH alone has 4,546 distinct values, so such a match by chance is very unlikely, and 41 of them is not credible. These rows are treated as recording duplicates.

They matter for two reasons. A duplicated hour gets double weight in training. Worse, after a random split one copy can land in the training set and the other in the test set, so the model is scored on a record it has already seen. That inflates the test score, which is a form of leakage.

The reference paper (Santarisi and Faouri, 2021) reported no duplicates.

In [14]:
log("Duplicates", f"{n_dup} exact duplicate rows ({n_dup / len(raw):.2%}), no conflicting targets",
    "drop the second copy of each")

3.5 Physical limits¶

Each variable is compared with the limits that physics or the plant allows:

  • RH is a ratio of vapour pressure to saturation pressure and cannot exceed 100%.
  • AT, AP and RH must lie in a plausible range for ambient air at a site near sea level.
  • PE must be positive and below the plant's full-load output.
In [15]:
limits = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "physical lower": [-30, 0, 950, 0, 0],
        "physical upper": [55, np.nan, 1060, 100, np.nan],
    },
    index=EXPECTED_COLUMNS,
)
limits["observed min"] = raw.min()
limits["observed max"] = raw.max()
limits["rows below"] = [(raw[c] < limits.loc[c, "physical lower"]).sum() for c in EXPECTED_COLUMNS]
limits["rows above"] = [(raw[c] > limits.loc[c, "physical upper"]).sum()
                        if pd.notna(limits.loc[c, "physical upper"]) else 0 for c in EXPECTED_COLUMNS]

55 rows report RH above 100%, at most 100.16%. These are small sensor overshoots on saturated (foggy or rainy) hours, which also explains why they occur on colder-than-average hours. The other four values in each row are normal. Deleting the rows would throw away valid measurements of AT, V, AP and PE because of an error of 0.16 percentage points in RH, so section 4 caps RH at 100% instead.

All other variables are within physical limits.

3.6 Units¶

Units are not stated inside the file. They come from the dataset description: °C, cm Hg, mbar, % and MW. The value ranges agree with these units for AT, AP, RH and PE. V does not fit:

182 hours have V above the ambient pressure of that same hour. A condenser vacuum, or a condenser absolute pressure, cannot exceed the pressure of the surrounding air, so V cannot be in cm Hg as labelled. The original paper does not explain this, and the true unit cannot be recovered from the data.

This does not harm the models. Any unit conversion is a linear rescaling, and section 6 standardizes every input, which removes it. The sign of the relationship (higher V, lower PE) is also unaffected. The issue limits interpretation only: section 12 treats V as a relative index of steam turbine back pressure and avoids quoting it as a physical pressure.

3.7 Outliers¶

Two standard rules are applied to every column: the IQR rule (outside Q1 - 1.5 IQR or Q3 + 1.5 IQR) and the z-score rule (more than 3 standard deviations from the mean). A flagged value is a statistical outlier. Whether it is an error is an engineering question, answered below.

In [19]:
rows = []
for c in EXPECTED_COLUMNS:
    q1, q3 = raw[c].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    z = (raw[c] - raw[c].mean()) / raw[c].std()
    rows.append({
        "IQR fence low": low, "IQR fence high": high,
        "IQR outliers low": (raw[c] < low).sum(), "IQR outliers high": (raw[c] > high).sum(),
        "|z| > 3": (z.abs() > 3).sum(),
    })
outliers = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=EXPECTED_COLUMNS).round(2)
outliers

AP outliers: 88 rows, AP 992.9 to 1033.3 mbar

AT, V and PE have no outliers by either rule. The flagged AP values (about 993 to 997 mbar and 1030 to 1033 mbar) are ordinary low- and high-pressure weather systems; sea-level pressure regularly spans 980 to 1040 mbar. The flagged RH values (about 26 to 31%) are dry, hot hours. In every flagged row the output is inside the normal range of PE.

These are real operating conditions, not errors. They are also the conditions where a model is most likely to be wrong, because they are rare in the training data. Removing them would make the test score look better while making the model worse at exactly the hours an operator would want it for. All outliers are kept. They lie just outside the fences (AP within about 2% of its median), so they do not distort the scaling in section 6.

3.8 Target distribution (imbalance check)¶

Class imbalance applies to classification. The regression equivalent is uneven coverage of the target range: if few hours have very high or very low output, the models see few examples there.

3.9 Correlation between inputs (multicollinearity)¶

The variance inflation factor (VIF) measures how well each input can be predicted from the other three. It is computed from the inverse of the input correlation matrix. VIF above 5 is a common warning level and above 10 is serious.

In [23]:
corr = raw.corr()
display(corr.round(3))

inputs_corr = raw[FEATURES].corr().to_numpy()
vif = pd.Series(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(inputs_corr)), index=FEATURES, name="VIF").round(2)
display(vif.to_frame())

log("Multicollinearity", f"AT-V r = {corr.loc['AT', 'V']:.2f}; max VIF {vif.max():.1f} ({vif.idxmax()})",
    "keep all four inputs; interpret AT and V effects jointly (section 12)")
AT V AP RH PE

V 0.844 1.000 -0.414 -0.312 -0.870
AP -0.508 -0.414 1.000 0.100 0.518
RH -0.543 -0.312 0.100 1.000 0.390
PE -0.948 -0.870 0.518 0.390 1.000
VIF
AT 5.98
V 3.94
AP 1.45
RH 1.71

AT and V are strongly correlated (r = 0.84), for the physical reason given in section 2.2: hot weather warms the condenser cooling and raises the back pressure. AT has a VIF of about 6, above the warning level of 5 but well below 10; V is about 4 and AP and RH are below 2. This is moderate multicollinearity. None of the three chosen models (SVR, KNN, MLP) needs uncorrelated inputs to fit well, so all four inputs are kept. The correlation does matter for interpretation: when AT rises, V usually rises too, so their separate effects have to be read with care in section 12.

3.10 Leakage review¶

Leakage is any route by which information about the test targets reaches the model during training. The sources checked are:

  • Columns derived from the target: none. All four inputs are independent sensor readings, recorded at the same time as PE.
  • ID or time columns that could encode the target: none.
  • Duplicate rows that could appear in both training and test sets: 41 found (section 3.4), removed in section 4.
  • Combining the five Excel sheets: would copy every row five times; not done (section 3.3).
  • Preprocessing fitted on all data before the split (scaling, any statistic-based cleaning): avoided by putting the scaler inside a scikit-learn pipeline that is fitted on training folds only (section 6).
  • Tuning hyperparameters on the test set: avoided by tuning with cross-validation on the training set only; the test set is used once, at the end.
In [24]:
log("Leakage", "no target-derived, ID or time columns; duplicates and sheet stacking are the only data-level risks",
    "remove duplicates; scaler inside pipeline; tune by CV on training data; test set used once")

4. Cleaning and preprocessing¶

Section 3 found two problems that need a change to the data and several that need none. The decisions are:

  1. Drop the 41 duplicate rows, keeping the first copy of each.
  2. Cap RH at 100%, keeping the 55 rows.
  3. Keep every outlier.
  4. Keep V unchanged.

Both changes are fixed rules: "remove exact repeats" and "RH cannot exceed 100%". Neither one uses a statistic computed from the data, such as a mean or a percentile. So they can be applied before the train/test split without leaking test information. Steps that do learn from the data, such as scaling, are fitted later, inside the pipeline, on training data only (section 6).

Every change is recorded row by row, so each value in the cleaned file can be traced back to the raw file.

4.1 Apply the cleaning rules¶

In [26]:
clean = raw.copy()
changes = []                            # row-level record of every change

# rule 1: exact duplicates, keep the first occurrence
dup_mask = clean.duplicated(keep="first")
for idx in clean.index[dup_mask]:
    first = clean.index[(clean == clean.loc[idx]).all(axis=1)][0]
    changes.append({"raw_index": idx, "column": "all", "old_value": np.nan, "new_value": np.nan,
                    "action": f"row removed: exact duplicate of raw_index {first}"})
clean = clean[~dup_mask]

# rule 2: relative humidity cannot exceed 100 %
RH_MAX = 100.0
rh_mask = clean["RH"] > RH_MAX
for idx in clean.index[rh_mask]:
    changes.append({"raw_index": idx, "column": "RH", "old_value": clean.at[idx, "RH"],
                    "new_value": RH_MAX, "action": "capped at the physical limit"})
clean.loc[rh_mask, "RH"] = RH_MAX

changes = pd.DataFrame(changes)
print(f"Rows removed (duplicates): {dup_mask.sum()}")
print(f"Values capped (RH > 100%): {rh_mask.sum()}")
print(f"Rows before: {len(raw):,}   rows after: {len(clean):,}")

Rows removed (duplicates): 41
Values capped (RH > 100%): 55
Rows before: 9,568   rows after: 9,527

raw_index is the zero-based row position in raw_data.csv (row 0 is the first data row below the header).

4.2 Verify the result¶

The checks below confirm that the rules did what was intended and nothing else.

In [27]:
assert clean.duplicated().sum() == 0, "duplicates remain"
assert clean["RH"].max() <= RH_MAX, "RH still above 100"
assert clean.isna().sum().sum() == 0, "missing values introduced"
assert len(clean) == len(raw) - dup_mask.sum(), "unexpected row count"

# every value that was not deliberately changed must equal the raw value
untouched = clean.drop(columns="RH").equals(raw.loc[clean.index].drop(columns="RH"))
rh_same = (clean.loc[~rh_mask, "RH"] == raw.loc[clean.index[~rh_mask], "RH"]).all()
assert untouched and rh_same, "a value changed that should not have"

print("All checks passed:")
print("  no duplicates, RH <= 100 %, no missing values, row count correct,")
print("  and every value not covered by a rule is identical to the raw data.")

Cleaning moves no column mean by more than 0.03 (in that column's unit), and no correlation coefficient by more than 0.003. That is the expected outcome. The duplicates are 0.4% of the rows and the RH corrections are at most 0.16 percentage points. Neither change hides a real feature of the data. Their value is in correctness: the test score can no longer be inflated by repeated rows, and no input is physically impossible.

4.4 What was deliberately not done¶

  • Outliers were not removed or clipped. They are real weather (section 3.7), and removing them would hide the hours where the models are least certain.
  • V was not converted or rescaled. Its true unit cannot be recovered (section 3.6), and standardization in section 6 makes the unit irrelevant to the models.
  • No rows were dropped for being difficult to predict.
  • Scaling and feature engineering are not applied here. They depend on statistics of the data, so they are fitted inside the modelling pipeline on training data only (section 6). The cleaned file therefore keeps every value in its original physical unit, which is also what the Tableau dashboard needs.

5. Exploratory visualizations and engineering insights¶

The charts in this section use the cleaned data. They are chosen to answer engineering questions, not to show every possible plot:

  1. What range of conditions does the plant see? (5.1)
  2. How does output respond to each input, and is the response linear? (5.2)
  3. Which correlations are real effects and which are borrowed from temperature? (5.3)
  4. What does the condenser add on top of temperature? (5.4)
  5. What is left after temperature is accounted for? (5.5)
  6. Why does output have two clusters? (5.6)

Section 5.7 states the engineering insights that follow.

In [31]:
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

SEQ = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("seq_blue", ["#d6e6f8", "#2a78d6", "#0d3b73"])
DIV = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div_blue_orange", ["#2a78d6", "#f2f1ee", "#eb6834"])
LABELS = {"AT": "Ambient temperature AT (°C)", "V": "Exhaust vacuum V (cm Hg, as labelled)",
          "AP": "Ambient pressure AP (mbar)", "RH": "Relative humidity RH (%)",
          "PE": "Net electrical output PE (MW)"}


def binned_mean(x, y, bins):
    # mean of y in each x-bin, with the bin centre and a 95% interval of the mean
    groups = y.groupby(pd.cut(x, bins), observed=True)
    out = groups.agg(["mean", "std", "size"])
    out["centre"] = [iv.mid for iv in out.index]
    out["ci"] = 1.96 * out["std"] / np.sqrt(out["size"])
    return out[out["size"] >= 20]

5.1 Operating envelope: distributions of the inputs¶

In [32]:

    ax.axvline(clean[c].median(), color=C_REF, lw=1.2, ls="--")

AT covers a full annual cycle, from cold winter hours near 2 °C to summer hours above 35 °C. V is clearly bimodal: one group sits near 40 cm Hg and a second spreads from about 58 to 75 cm Hg, with few hours in between. AP is a narrow, near-normal distribution typical of a site near sea level. RH is skewed towards humid conditions, with a median near 75%.

5.2 Output against each input¶

In [33]:

Average slope of PE against AT: -2.17 MW per °C (-0.48% of mean output per °C)
Scatter of PE around a straight-line AT trend: 5.43 MW; around a curved trend: 5.20 MW

AT has the tightest relationship with output: about 2.2 MW lost per degree, roughly 0.5% of output per °C. Even so, at any single temperature the output still scatters by about ±5 MW (one standard deviation), so temperature alone cannot reach the 1% accuracy target. The other inputs have to explain that scatter.

The binned means also show that the responses are not straight lines. The PE-AT curve is slightly convex. The PE-V curve falls steeply between about 40 and 50 cm Hg and flattens above 70. The PE-AP curve is not even monotonic at the low-pressure end. Linear models would miss this, which is one reason the project uses nonlinear models.

5.3 Correlation: direct and partial¶

The ordinary (Pearson) correlation between an input and PE mixes the input's own effect with the effect of anything it moves together with. The partial correlation removes the linear influence of the other three inputs, so it shows each input's own association with PE. It is computed from the inverse of the correlation matrix.

In [35]:
pearson = clean.corr()
precision = np.linalg.inv(pearson.to_numpy())
d = np.sqrt(np.diag(precision))
partial_arr = -precision / np.outer(d, d)
np.fill_diagonal(partial_arr, 1.0)
partial = pd.DataFrame(partial_arr, index=pearson.index, columns=pearson.columns)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.3))
for ax, mat, title in [(axes[0], pearson, "Pearson correlation"),
                       (axes[1], partial, "Partial correlation (other inputs held fixed)")]:
    sns.heatmap(mat, ax=ax, cmap=DIV, vmin=-1, vmax=1, annot=True, fmt=".2f", square=True,
                linewidths=2, linecolor="white", cbar=ax is axes[1],
                annot_kws={"fontsize": 9, "color": C_INK})
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig06_correlation_heatmaps.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

display(pd.DataFrame({"Pearson r with PE": pearson[TARGET], "partial r with PE": partial[TARGET]})
        .drop(TARGET).round(3))
Pearson r with PE partial r with PE
AT -0.948 -0.797
V -0.870 -0.314
AP 0.519 0.065
RH 0.391 -0.360

Two inputs change their story once the others are held fixed:

  • RH reverses sign. Its plain correlation with output is positive (+0.39), but its partial correlation is negative (-0.36). Humid hours are mostly cool hours (r(AT, RH) = -0.54), and cool hours give high output. Once temperature is accounted for, more humidity means less output.
  • AP almost disappears. Its plain correlation (+0.52) drops to about +0.07. High-pressure weather here tends to be cold weather, so most of AP's apparent effect is really temperature.

AT stays strongly negative and V keeps a moderate negative partial correlation, so both have effects of their own.

5.4 Temperature and the condenser together¶

hours mean V std of V r(PE, V) inside band
AT
(0, 10] 1144.0 40.31 2.83 -0.17
(10, 15] 1908.0 42.10 3.92 -0.31

Two things stand out. First, V rises with temperature: the condenser runs at a higher back pressure on hot days, because its cooling medium is warmer. Second, within a temperature band, hours with a higher V give lower output. This is the vertical colour gradient at a fixed AT. The table shows that this within-band link is weak below 10 °C and above 30 °C, where V hardly varies (near 40 in the cold, near 70 in the heat), and strongest between 15 and 30 °C (r between -0.53 and -0.66), where V spreads widely.

So the condenser costs output mainly in warm weather. The effect of V depends on AT, which is an interaction between inputs. Models that can learn interactions (SVR with an RBF kernel, KNN, MLP) are suited to this; a model that adds up separate input effects is not.

5.5 What remains after temperature¶

To see the secondary inputs clearly, the curved AT trend from 5.2 is subtracted from PE. The remainder is the output above or below what temperature alone would suggest. It is plotted against RH, AP and V as binned means with 95% intervals. The curve fit is a descriptive tool for this chart only, not one of the project's models.

In [37]:

    ax.errorbar(bm["centre"], bm["mean"], yerr=bm["ci"], color=C_MAIN, lw=2, marker="o",
                markersize=5, capsize=3)

    ax.set_xlabel(LABELS[c])

  • RH: the remainder falls steadily from about +4 MW on dry hours (35 to 45% RH) to about -3.5 MW on saturated hours, a swing of about 8 MW. This is the clearest and most consistent secondary effect in the data.
  • AP: the remainder rises by about 3 to 4 MW between 1003 and 1015 mbar, then drifts back down above 1020 mbar. There is no consistent direction across the whole range, so AP's own effect is small and uncertain.
  • V: roughly level (within about 2 MW of zero) up to about 66, then a dip to nearly -4 MW around V = 70. The condenser penalty behaves like a threshold, not a straight line.

hours AT V AP RH PE
V < 52 4738 14.0 42.7 1015.1 77.8 467.8

Splitting the hours at V = 52 separates the two output clusters almost cleanly. The low-V regime is the cool season: mean AT about 14 °C, mean output about 468 MW. The high-V regime is the warm season: mean AT about 25 °C, mean output about 441 MW, condenser at high back pressure, low output. The bimodal shape of PE found in section 3.8 is therefore a seasonal effect carried through both the gas turbine (AT) and the condenser (V). The models have to work in both regimes, which is why section 6 stratifies the split by output band.

5.7 Engineering insights¶

In [39]:
insight_numbers = {
    "MW per °C of AT": trend[1][0],
    "PE gap, coldest vs hottest 5% of hours (MW)":
        clean.loc[clean["AT"] <= clean["AT"].quantile(0.05), TARGET].mean()
        - clean.loc[clean["AT"] >= clean["AT"].quantile(0.95), TARGET].mean(),
    "scatter of PE at fixed AT (MW, 1 std)": resid_std[2],
    "Pearson r(RH, PE)": pearson.loc["RH", TARGET],
    "partial r(RH, PE)": partial.loc["RH", TARGET],
    "RH effect at fixed AT, dry to saturated (MW)": effects["RH"],
    "Pearson r(AP, PE)": pearson.loc["AP", TARGET],
    "partial r(AP, PE)": partial.loc["AP", TARGET],
    "V effect at fixed AT (MW)": effects["V"],
}
pd.Series(insight_numbers).round(2).to_frame("value")
Out[39]:
value
MW per °C of AT -2.17
PE gap, coldest vs hottest 5% of hours (MW) 52.55
scatter of PE at fixed AT (MW, 1 std) 5.20
Pearson r(RH, PE) 0.39
partial r(RH, PE) -0.36
RH effect at fixed AT, dry to saturated (MW) 8.10
Pearson r(AP, PE) 0.52
partial r(AP, PE) 0.07
V effect at fixed AT (MW) 5.53

  1. Ambient temperature sets the plant's capacity. Each extra degree costs about 2.2 MW, around 0.5% of output, and the hottest hours deliver about 52 MW less than the coldest. Most of this follows from the falling density of the compressor inlet air (section 2.2). For operations, the plant's sellable capacity on a hot afternoon is well below its winter capacity, and commitments to the grid should follow the temperature forecast. Inlet air cooling would act directly on the largest loss.

  2. The condenser matters mainly in warm weather. Below about 10 °C, V stays near 40 and has little effect. Between 15 and 30 °C, V spreads widely, and at the same temperature higher V means lower output. The loss appears mostly above V ≈ 66, which is a threshold, not a straight line. Condenser cleaning and cooling-system maintenance therefore pay off most before and during summer.

  3. Humid air lowers output once temperature is accounted for. RH correlates positively with PE (+0.39) only because humid hours are cool hours. At a fixed temperature the effect is negative (partial r = -0.36), worth about 8 MW between dry and saturated air. This agrees with the physics: water vapour is lighter than dry air, so humid air carries less mass through the compressor. Reading the plain correlation at face value would have suggested the opposite.

  4. Pressure's apparent effect is mostly borrowed from temperature. AP's correlation of +0.52 drops to about +0.07 when the other inputs are held fixed. Its own effect is a few MW at most, with no consistent direction across the normal weather range. A model that ranked AP as the second most useful input on correlation alone would be misleading.

  5. The data has two seasonal operating regimes, and the relationships are nonlinear and interacting. Output splits into a cool, low-V regime and a warm, high-V regime. The response to AT is curved, the response to V has a threshold, and the effect of V depends on AT. This is the evidence for choosing nonlinear models that learn interactions (SVR, KNN, MLP) over linear ones, and for checking the error separately in each output band.

Sections 10 and 12 test whether the trained models reproduce insights 1 to 4.

6. Feature preparation and data split¶

This section fixes everything the three models share, so that sections 7 to 9 compare models on equal terms:

  • the inputs and the target,
  • one train/test split, with the test set locked away until the final evaluation,
  • scaling inside a pipeline, so that it never sees validation or test data,
  • the cross-validation scheme and the metrics,
  • a trivial baseline that every model must beat,
  • a test of one physics-based feature: the density of the inlet air.
In [40]:
import time
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import (mean_absolute_error, root_mean_squared_error,
                             mean_absolute_percentage_error, r2_score)

6.1 Train/test split¶

The data has no timestamps (section 2.3), so a chronological split is not possible and a randomized split is the correct choice. 80% of the hours are used for training and tuning, and 20% (about 1,900 hours) form the test set.

The split is stratified on output deciles. Section 3.8 showed that PE has two clusters and thin tails. Stratifying guarantees that every part of the output range, including the rare high and low hours, appears in the test set in the same proportion as in the whole dataset.

The test set is used exactly once, in section 10, after all tuning is finished.

In [41]:

y = clean[TARGET]

TEST_SIZE = 0.20

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=TEST_SIZE, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=pe_decile
)

# leakage checks: no row in both sets, and no identical record in both sets
assert set(X_train.index).isdisjoint(X_test.index)
overlap = pd.merge(clean.loc[X_train.index], clean.loc[X_test.index], how="inner", on=EXPECTED_COLUMNS)

print(f"Test set:     {len(X_test):,} hours ({len(X_test) / len(X):.0%})")

6.2 Scaling¶

The inputs have very different scales: AP varies by a few mbar around 1,013, while V spans more than 50 units. All three models need comparable scales:

  • KNN measures distances between hours. Without scaling, the input with the largest spread would dominate the distance.
  • SVR with an RBF kernel also works on distances, so the same applies.
  • The MLP trains by gradient descent, which converges slowly and unevenly when inputs differ in scale.

StandardScaler is used: it subtracts each input's mean and divides by its standard deviation. A robust scaler (median and IQR) is not needed because section 3.7 found only mild outliers in AP and RH.

In [44]:
scale_check = pd.DataFrame({"mean": X_train.mean(), "std": X_train.std(),
                            "range": X_train.max() - X_train.min()}).round(2)
scale_check
Out[44]:
mean std range
AT 19.67 7.46 35.30
V 54.27 12.69 56.20
AP 1013.23 5.96 40.41
RH 73.30 14.63 74.11

To avoid leakage, the scaler is not fitted on the whole dataset. It is the first step of a scikit-learn Pipeline. Each time the pipeline is fitted, whether on a cross-validation fold or on the full training set, the scaler learns its mean and standard deviation from that training data only, and then applies them unchanged to the held-out data.

In [45]:
def make_pipeline(estimator):
    # scaler + model; fitted as one object so the scaler only ever sees training data
    return Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("model", estimator)])

6.3 Validation scheme and metrics¶

Hyperparameters are tuned with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. The training set is shuffled and cut into five folds; each fold is held out once while the model is trained on the other four. The mean over the five folds is the model's validation score, and the spread across folds shows how stable it is.

Four metrics are reported, each answering a different question:

  • MAE (MW): the typical size of an error.
  • RMSE (MW): like MAE but weights large errors more. It is the main tuning metric, because large errors are the costly ones when committing output to the grid.
  • MAPE (%): error relative to output, used for the 1% target in section 2.5.
  • R²: the share of the variation in output that the model explains.

MSE is not reported separately: it is RMSE squared, in MW², and adds no information.

In [46]:
N_FOLDS = 5
cv = KFold(n_splits=N_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

SCORING = {
    "MAE": "neg_mean_absolute_error",
    "RMSE": "neg_root_mean_squared_error",
    "MAPE": "neg_mean_absolute_percentage_error",
    "R2": "r2",
}


def cv_summary(estimator, X_, y_, label):
    # cross-validated metrics for one pipeline, as a one-row dataframe
    res = cross_validate(estimator, X_, y_, cv=cv, scoring=SCORING, n_jobs=-1, return_train_score=True)
    row = {"model": label}
    for m in SCORING:
        sign = 1 if m == "R2" else -1
        scale = 100 if m == "MAPE" else 1
        row[f"CV {m}"] = sign * res[f"test_{m}"].mean() * scale
        row[f"CV {m} std"] = res[f"test_{m}"].std() * scale
    row["train RMSE"] = abs(res["train_RMSE"].mean())
    row["fit time (s)"] = res["fit_time"].mean()
    return pd.DataFrame([row]).set_index("model")


def evaluate(y_true, y_pred):
    # the four metrics for a set of predictions
    return {
        "MAE": mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred),
        "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred),
        "MAPE %": 100 * mean_absolute_percentage_error(y_true, y_pred),
        "R2": r2_score(y_true, y_pred),
    }

6.4 Baseline¶

A model that ignores the inputs and always predicts the mean training output sets the floor. Any useful model must be far better.

baseline_cv.round(3)

6.5 Physics-based feature: inlet air density¶

Section 2.2 argued that AT, AP and RH act on the gas turbine mainly through one quantity: the density of the air entering the compressor. That density can be computed for each hour from the three measurements.

Moist air is treated as a mixture of ideal gases, dry air and water vapour:

$$\rho = \frac{p_d}{R_d\,T} + \frac{p_v}{R_v\,T}, \qquad p_v = \frac{RH}{100}\,p_{sat}(T), \qquad p_d = p - p_v$$

with $R_d$ = 287.058 J/(kg·K), $R_v$ = 461.495 J/(kg·K) and $T$ in kelvin. The saturation vapour pressure uses the Magnus formula, $p_{sat}$ = 6.112 exp(17.62 t / (243.12 + t)) hPa, with t in °C.

The feature is a fixed formula applied row by row and uses no statistics of the data, so it cannot leak test information. Here the question is whether it helps the models. That is tested by cross-validating each of the three model types on three input sets:

  • the four measured inputs,
  • the four inputs plus density,
  • density and V only (one variable for the gas turbine side and one for the steam side).

The model settings here are fixed, reasonable starting values, not tuned ones. The comparison is between input sets with the same model, so tuning is not needed for a fair answer; sections 7 to 9 tune each model on the chosen inputs.

In [48]:
R_DRY, R_VAP = 287.058, 461.495        # J/(kg K)


def add_air_density(df):
    out = df.copy()
    t = out["AT"]
    p_sat = 6.112 * np.exp(17.62 * t / (243.12 + t))        # hPa (= mbar)
    p_v = out["RH"] / 100 * p_sat
    p_d = out["AP"] - p_v
    T = t + 273.15
    out["RHO"] = (p_d * 100) / (R_DRY * T) + (p_v * 100) / (R_VAP * T)   # kg/m3
    return out


X_train_rho = add_air_density(X_train)
print(f"Air density: {X_train_rho['RHO'].min():.3f} to {X_train_rho['RHO'].max():.3f} kg/m³")
print(f"r(RHO, PE) = {X_train_rho['RHO'].corr(y_train):+.3f}   r(AT, PE) = {X_train['AT'].corr(y_train):+.3f}"
      f"   r(RHO, AT) = {X_train_rho['RHO'].corr(X_train['AT']):+.3f}")

Air density: 1.121 to 1.298 kg/m³
r(RHO, PE) = +0.947   r(AT, PE) = -0.948   r(RHO, AT) = -0.984
In [49]:
screen_models = {
    "SVR": SVR(kernel="rbf", C=10),
    "KNN": KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=10, weights="distance"),
    "MLP": MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 64), early_stopping=True, max_iter=1000,
                        random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}

        res = cv_summary(make_pipeline(est), X_train_rho[cols], y_train, m_name)
        rows.append({"model": m_name, "inputs": s_name,

RMSE change from adding density (positive = better):
  KNN: +0.038 MW   (fold-to-fold std of RMSE about 0.25 MW)
  MLP: +0.014 MW   (fold-to-fold std of RMSE about 0.22 MW)
  SVR: -0.003 MW   (fold-to-fold std of RMSE about 0.24 MW)

Density is almost a mirror image of temperature (r(RHO, AT) close to -1). Adding it to the four inputs changes the cross-validated RMSE by a few hundredths of a MW at most for each model, which is far smaller than the spread between folds. The nonlinear models already combine AT, AP and RH internally, so a hand-made combination of the same three measurements gives them nothing new.

The two-input set (density and V) is worth a note. With one variable for the gas turbine side and one for the steam side, the models lose only about half a MW of RMSE compared with all four inputs. This supports the physics in section 2.2: most of what the ambient conditions do to the plant passes through inlet air density.

Decision: the models use the four measured inputs. Density is not added, because it does not improve accuracy and adds a derived quantity that must be computed and explained. The test stays in the notebook as evidence for this choice.

7. Model 1: support vector regression (SVR)¶

Sections 7 to 9 follow the same pattern for each model: why it suits this problem, how it was tuned, its cross-validated performance, a check for overfitting, and an analysis of its errors. All of this uses the training set only. The three tuned models meet the test set together in section 10, so none of them is chosen or adjusted using test results.

In [52]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.base import clone

best_models = {}        # tuned pipelines, one per model, for sections 10 to 13
cv_tables = {}          # cross-validated metrics of each tuned model
oof_predictions = {}    # out-of-fold predictions on the training set


def grid_table(search, params):
    # tidy table of a grid search: one row per setting, sorted by CV RMSE
    res = pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_)
    cols = [f"param_model__{p}" for p in params]
    out = res[cols + ["mean_test_score", "std_test_score", "mean_fit_time"]].copy()
    out.columns = params + ["CV RMSE", "CV RMSE std", "fit time (s)"]
    out["CV RMSE"] = -out["CV RMSE"]
    return out.sort_values("CV RMSE").reset_index(drop=True)


def residual_diagnostics(name, y_true, y_pred, fig_name):
    # predicted vs actual, and error against temperature, from out-of-fold predictions
    err = y_pred - y_true
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4))
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.scatter(y_true, y_pred, s=4, alpha=0.3, color=C_MAIN, linewidths=0)
    lims = [y_true.min() - 2, y_true.max() + 2]
    ax.plot(lims, lims, color=C_REF, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="perfect prediction")
    ax.set(xlim=lims, ylim=lims, xlabel="Actual PE (MW)", ylabel="Predicted PE (MW)",
           title=f"{name}: predicted against actual (out-of-fold)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.scatter(X_train["AT"], err, s=4, alpha=0.3, color=C_MAIN, linewidths=0)
    bm = binned_mean(X_train["AT"], err, np.arange(0, 40, 2))
    ax.plot(bm["centre"], bm["mean"], color=C_FLAG, lw=2, label="binned mean error")
    ax.axhline(0, color=C_REF, lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set(xlabel=LABELS["AT"], ylabel="Prediction error (MW)", title=f"{name}: error against temperature")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / fig_name, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()

    bands = pd.cut(y_true, np.arange(420, 501, 10))
    by_band = pd.DataFrame({"abs error": err.abs(), "error": err}).groupby(bands, observed=True).agg(
        hours=("error", "size"), MAE=("abs error", "mean"), mean_error=("error", "mean"))
    by_band.columns = ["hours", "MAE (MW)", "mean error (MW)"]
    return by_band.round(2)

7.1 Why SVR suits this problem¶

Support vector regression fits a function that keeps as many training hours as possible inside a tube of half-width ε around it. Errors smaller than ε cost nothing, and larger errors are penalized linearly, with weight C. With the RBF (Gaussian) kernel the function can bend smoothly in any direction, so it can follow the curved AT response and the AT-V interaction found in section 5.

Reasons it fits this dataset:

  • The relationships are smooth and nonlinear (section 5). The RBF kernel produces smooth curves, which matches the physics of air density and condenser pressure. It will not produce the steps that a tree-based model would.
  • The ε-tube ignores small errors. Hourly averages of plant sensors carry some noise, and ε can be set in MW to roughly match it, so the model does not chase noise.
  • There are only 4 inputs and about 7,600 training hours. The cost of kernel methods grows quickly with the number of rows, but at this size training takes seconds.
  • There are three hyperparameters, and each has a clear meaning: C (how strongly large errors are penalized), γ (how local the kernel is; larger γ means a more flexible curve) and ε (the width of the tolerance in MW).

Weaknesses to keep in mind: SVR needs scaled inputs (handled by the pipeline), it does not scale well to very large datasets, and the fitted model is hard to read directly. Section 12 uses model-agnostic tools for interpretation.

7.2 Tuning C and γ¶

A grid search over C and γ with ε fixed at 0.5 MW, using the 5-fold cross-validation from section 6. The range was set by a coarser search during development, which showed the optimum lies between C = 10 and 100 and between γ = 0.5 and 4. Large C with large γ is slow to train, so the grid stops at C = 100.

In [53]:

    "model__epsilon": [0.5],
}

The error surface has a clear valley. Small γ gives a curve that is too stiff to follow the AT-V interaction, so error is high on the left. Very large γ makes each training hour influence only its close neighbours, so the curve starts to follow noise, and error rises again on the right. Raising C helps up to a point and then flattens out.

7.3 Tuning ε¶

With C and γ fixed at their best values, ε is varied. ε is the half-width of the zone, in MW, where errors are not penalized.

Support vectors (training hours that define the model): {0.1: '7,415 (97%)', 0.25: '7,050 (93%)', 0.5: '6,505 (85%)', 1.0: '5,524 (72%)', 2.0: '3,960 (52%)', 3.0: '2,836 (37%)'}

ε has only a small effect on accuracy across a wide range, which is a sign of a stable model. It has a large effect on model size: a wider tube leaves more training hours strictly inside it, and those hours drop out of the model. The best ε is about 1 to 2 MW, and the larger value also roughly halves the number of support vectors compared with ε = 0.1. An ε of 2 MW means errors under about 0.4% of output are treated as noise, which is a reasonable tolerance for hourly-averaged plant measurements.

The gap between training and cross-validation error measures overfitting: a model that memorizes the training hours has a small training error and a much larger validation error. A modest gap, with fold-to-fold spread of a few tenths of a MW, means the SVR generalizes well to hours it has not seen.

7.5 Where the SVR makes its errors¶

Out-of-fold predictions are used here: every training hour is predicted by the model fitted on the four folds that did not contain it. This gives an honest error for every training hour without touching the test set.

The predicted-against-actual plot lies along the diagonal over the whole output range, and the error shows no systematic trend with temperature: the binned mean error stays close to zero from cold to hot hours. The table by output band shows where accuracy is weaker. Errors are largest in the sparse bands at the extremes, where there are fewer training hours to learn from, and the mean error there is pulled towards the middle of the range. This is a typical pattern for a smooth regression model and is checked again on the test set in section 10.

Error here means predicted minus actual, so a positive error is an over-prediction. A small number of hours have errors far larger than the rest, visible as isolated points above the diagonal (left) and far above zero (right). Almost all of them are over-predictions: the plant produced roughly 24 to 48 MW less than the model expected. Their inputs are ordinary, and many are cool hours where the plant would normally be near its highest output. The weather cannot explain the shortfall, so something inside the plant must have: a partial trip, a unit running below full load for part of the hour, or another disturbance not recorded in the data.

No model using these four inputs can predict such hours, and they were deliberately not removed (section 4.4). They are also a direct demonstration of the condition-monitoring use in section 2.4: a measured output far below the model's expectation is exactly the signal an operator would want flagged for investigation.

8. Model 2: k-nearest neighbours regression (KNN)¶

8.1 Why KNN suits this problem¶

KNN makes no assumption about the shape of the relationship. To predict the output for a new hour, it finds the k training hours with the most similar conditions (AT, V, AP, RH after scaling) and averages their outputs. With distance weighting, closer hours count more.

Reasons it fits this dataset:

  • It is the most direct form of engineering reasoning: "the last times the plant ran in conditions like these, it produced about this much". Operators can check a prediction by looking at the actual hours behind it.
  • The data covers six years of full-load operation densely. With about 7,600 training hours in only four dimensions, most new hours have close neighbours.
  • It can follow any nonlinear shape and any interaction, including the threshold in V and the AT-V interaction from section 5, without being told about them.
  • Training is instant: the model simply stores the training hours. Prediction requires a neighbour search, which is fast at this size.

Weaknesses to keep in mind:

  • It cannot extrapolate. A prediction is an average of outputs the plant has already produced, so for conditions outside the training range (for example a 42 °C day), KNN returns the output of the nearest hours that do exist. Section 11 checks this.
  • Every scaled input counts equally in the distance, even though AT matters far more than AP. Section 8.4 checks whether the weak inputs help or hurt.
  • It needs scaled inputs, which the pipeline provides.

8.2 Tuning¶

Three hyperparameters are tuned together with the same 5-fold cross-validation:

  • k, the number of neighbours (1 to 30, then 40, 50, 75, 100),
  • weighting: every neighbour equal ("uniform"), or weighted by inverse distance ("distance"),
  • the distance measure: Manhattan (p = 1, the sum of absolute differences) or Euclidean (p = 2, the straight-line distance).
In [59]:

    "model__n_neighbors": list(range(1, 31)) + [40, 50, 75, 100],
    "model__weights": ["uniform", "distance"],
    "model__p": [1, 2],
}

The curve shows the bias-variance trade-off directly. With k = 1 the model copies the output of the single nearest hour, including that hour's measurement noise, so the error is high (overfitting). As k grows, noise averages out and the error falls to a minimum. Beyond that, the neighbourhood becomes so wide that it mixes hours from genuinely different conditions, and the prediction is smoothed too much (underfitting).

Distance weighting is better than equal weighting at every k above 1 (with one neighbour the two are identical): when the neighbourhood is wider than ideal, the far neighbours get less say. Manhattan distance is better than Euclidean for both weightings. Euclidean distance squares the differences, so one input that differs a lot dominates the distance. Manhattan distance adds the differences, so all four inputs contribute more evenly.

The training RMSE of the distance-weighted KNN is zero, and this is not a sign of anything wrong. When a training hour is predicted, it finds itself as its own nearest neighbour at distance zero, which receives all the weight. So the training error of a distance-weighted KNN is always zero and says nothing about overfitting. The honest measures here are the cross-validated error and its spread across folds, which are similar in size to those of the SVR.

8.4 Does every input help?¶

KNN gives every scaled input the same say in the distance. If an input carried no useful information, it would only add noise to the distance and make the neighbours worse. This is tested by removing one input at a time and cross-validating the tuned model on the other three.

In [62]:

knn_drop = pd.DataFrame(drop_rows)

3 without AP 4.059 0.420
4 without RH 3.775 0.136

Removing any input makes the model worse, so all four carry information the others do not. The ranking matches section 5: AT matters most by far, then V. AP and RH have smaller effects, but they still help, even though KNN gives them the same weight in the distance as AT. This agrees with insight 3 in section 5.7: humidity has a real effect once temperature is accounted for.

The pattern is similar to the SVR's: no trend of error with temperature, slightly larger errors in the sparse extreme bands, and a few hours with very large over-predictions. Most of those hours are the same ones the SVR could not predict. Two models built on completely different principles agree that these hours do not fit the weather, which strengthens the conclusion in section 7.5 that something inside the plant caused them.

9. Model 3: multilayer perceptron (MLP)¶

9.1 Why an MLP suits this problem¶

A multilayer perceptron is a feed-forward neural network. Each hidden layer applies a weighted sum of its inputs followed by a nonlinear activation (here ReLU, max(0, x)). Stacking layers lets the network build up curved responses and interactions from simple pieces. It is trained by gradient descent (the Adam optimizer) to minimize squared error.

Reasons it fits this dataset:

  • It is a universal approximator: with enough hidden units it can represent the curved AT response, the V threshold and the AT-V interaction from section 5 without being told about them.
  • Once trained, the model is a short sequence of matrix multiplications. Prediction is fast and the trained model is small (a few thousand weights), so it is easy to deploy in a plant monitoring system that receives sensor data every hour.
  • Unlike KNN, it does not store the training data, and unlike SVR, its training cost grows only linearly with the number of rows. It would scale to years of second-by-second sensor data.
  • The reference study avoided neural networks to keep its methods simple. Including one tests whether the extra flexibility is worth its cost here.

Weaknesses to keep in mind:

  • Training is stochastic. Results depend on the random initial weights, so section 9.5 checks how much they vary between seeds.
  • There are many design choices (layers, units, regularization, learning rate), so tuning costs more than for SVR or KNN.
  • The network is the hardest of the three to explain directly. Section 12 uses model-agnostic tools.
  • Like SVR, it can produce predictions outside the training range, which can be useful or dangerous. Section 11 checks this.

9.2 Design choices fixed before tuning¶

  • Inputs are standardized by the pipeline, as for the other models.
  • The target is standardized too. PE is around 450 MW with a spread of about 17 MW. Without scaling, the network's output layer has to learn a large offset first, and the training signal for the shape of the relationship is weak. TransformedTargetRegressor scales PE before training and converts predictions back to MW, using statistics from the training data only. The comparison below shows the effect.
  • Early stopping: 10% of each training fold is held back inside the MLP, and training stops when the error on that part has not improved for 30 epochs. This limits overfitting and saves time. The held-back hours come from the training fold, so no validation or test data is involved.
  • Activation ReLU, optimizer Adam, initial learning rate 0.001, at most 2,000 epochs.
In [65]:
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor


def make_mlp(hidden=(64, 64), alpha=1e-3, scale_target=True, seed=RANDOM_STATE):
    net = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=hidden, alpha=alpha, activation="relu", solver="adam",
                       learning_rate_init=1e-3, early_stopping=True, validation_fraction=0.1,
                       n_iter_no_change=30, max_iter=2000, random_state=seed)
    if scale_target:
        net = TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=net, transformer=StandardScaler())
    return make_pipeline(net)


target_check = pd.concat([
    cv_summary(make_mlp(scale_target=False), X_train, y_train, "MLP (64, 64), target in MW"),
    cv_summary(make_mlp(scale_target=True), X_train, y_train, "MLP (64, 64), target standardized"),
])

Standardizing the target lowers the error and also speeds up training, because the network converges in fewer epochs. All MLPs below use it.

9.3 Tuning architecture and regularization¶

The grid covers network size and the L2 penalty α. Larger α pushes weights towards zero, which gives a smoother function and less overfitting. The architectures range from two hidden layers of 64 units to three layers of 128, 128 and 64 units. (A two-layer (128, 64) network was also tried during development and fell between the first two.)

Two kinds of learning curve check whether the network is trained properly and whether more data would help.

  • The training history (left and middle) shows the loss on the training data and the R² on the early-stopping hold-out, epoch by epoch, for one fit on the full training set. Training should stop once the hold-out score levels off.
  • The learning curve (right) refits the tuned MLP on growing fractions of the training set and cross-validates each. If the validation error is still falling at 100%, more data would improve the model. If it has flattened and sits close to the training error, the model is limited by noise in the data, not by data volume.

The training loss drops steeply in the first few epochs and then keeps falling slowly. The hold-out R² rises quickly, levels off, and from then on only fluctuates. Early stopping ended training about 30 epochs after the best hold-out score, as intended, and the weights from the best epoch are the ones used.

The learning curve gives two messages. Training and cross-validated error are close at every size, so the network is not memorizing the data. The cross-validated error is still falling at the largest size, by roughly 0.2 MW between half and all of the training data, so more operating hours would still improve the MLP a little. For a plant that keeps logging data, the model could be retrained periodically as the record grows.

9.5 Sensitivity to the random seed¶

A neural network starts from random weights and sees the data in a random order, so two training runs with different seeds give slightly different models. The tuned MLP is cross-validated with three different seeds. If the spread is small compared with the differences between models, the comparison in section 10 is not an accident of one lucky seed.

The MLP's error pattern matches the other two models: no trend with temperature, larger errors in the sparse extreme bands with predictions pulled towards the middle, and a handful of large over-predictions, most of them on the same hours where SVR and KNN also fail.

9.7 What the MLP results show¶

  • Network size mattered more than regularization. Deeper and wider networks were better at every α, while changing α within each architecture moved the error by only a few hundredths of a MW. Early stopping already limits overfitting, and with about 7,600 hours for 4 inputs the data is plentiful, so the L2 penalty has little extra to do.
  • The tuned MLP reaches about the same accuracy as the tuned SVR. The difference between them is a few hundredths of a MW, which is about the size of the seed-to-seed variation in 9.5, so on this evidence the two are tied. KNN is ahead of both by about 0.15 to 0.2 MW in cross-validation.
  • The MLP is the most expensive model to train: tens of seconds per fit, against a few seconds for SVR and almost nothing for KNN. Its advantages are in deployment: it is small, fast to evaluate, and does not need the training data at prediction time.

Section 10 brings the three models together on the test set and makes the final choice.

10. Model comparison and final selection¶

This is the first and only time the test set is used. Each tuned model was fitted on the full training set in sections 7 to 9 and is now applied, unchanged, to the 1,906 test hours.

The comparison goes beyond a single accuracy number:

  1. accuracy on the test set, and whether it agrees with cross-validation (10.1),
  2. comparison with the reference study and the success criteria of section 2.5 (10.2),
  3. whether the differences between models are larger than chance (10.3),
  4. where in the output range each model makes its errors, and in which direction (10.4),
  5. robustness to sensor noise (10.5),
  6. behaviour outside the training range (10.6),
  7. a model for day-ahead use without V (10.7),
  8. cost and practicality (10.8).

Section 10.9 makes the choice.

10.1 Test-set accuracy¶

In [73]:
MODEL_ORDER = ["SVR", "KNN", "MLP"]
MODEL_COLORS = dict(zip(MODEL_ORDER, C_CAT[:3]))

test_pred = {}
pred_time = {}
for name in MODEL_ORDER:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    test_pred[name] = pd.Series(best_models[name].predict(X_test), index=y_test.index)
    pred_time[name] = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(X_test) * 1000 * 1000    # ms per 1,000 hours
test_pred["mean baseline"] = pd.Series(y_train.mean(), index=y_test.index)

rows = []
for name in MODEL_ORDER + ["mean baseline"]:
    m = evaluate(y_test, test_pred[name])
    row = {"model": name, **{f"test {k}": v for k, v in m.items()}}
    if name in cv_tables:
        row["CV RMSE"] = cv_tables[name]["CV RMSE"].iloc[0]
    else:
        row["CV RMSE"] = baseline_cv["CV RMSE"].iloc[0]
    rows.append(row)

test_table["test - CV RMSE"] = test_table["test RMSE"] - test_table["CV RMSE"]

10.2 Against the reference study and the success criteria¶

The reference study (Santarisi and Faouri, 2021) used the same dataset. Its best model, gradient boosting, reached R² = 0.912 and MAPE = 0.872%. Its test split differs from ours, so the comparison is indicative, not exact.

All three models meet the accuracy criteria from section 2.5 and improve on the reference study: R² of about 0.955 against 0.912, and MAPE of 0.54 to 0.60% against 0.872%. The overfitting check does not apply to KNN (its training error is always zero, section 8.3); its test and cross-validated errors agree, which is the relevant evidence.

The remaining criteria, physical plausibility and practical cost, are tested below.

10.3 Are the differences real?¶

The models differ by fractions of a MW. To see whether those gaps would survive a different sample of test hours, the test set is resampled with replacement 2,000 times (a paired bootstrap). For each resample, the RMSE of two models is computed on the same hours and the difference is recorded. If the 95% interval of the difference excludes zero, one model is genuinely better on data like this.

In [75]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)
n_boot = 2000
sq_err = {m: ((test_pred[m] - y_test) ** 2).to_numpy() for m in MODEL_ORDER}
idx = rng.integers(0, len(y_test), size=(n_boot, len(y_test)))

boot_rows = []
for a, b in [("KNN", "SVR"), ("KNN", "MLP"), ("MLP", "SVR")]:
    diff = np.sqrt(sq_err[a][idx].mean(axis=1)) - np.sqrt(sq_err[b][idx].mean(axis=1))
    lo, mid, hi = np.percentile(diff, [2.5, 50, 97.5])
    boot_rows.append({"comparison": f"RMSE {a} - RMSE {b}", "median (MW)": mid, "95% low": lo, "95% high": hi,
                      "conclusion": f"{a} better" if hi < 0 else (f"{b} better" if lo > 0 else "no clear difference")})
bootstrap_table = pd.DataFrame(boot_rows).set_index("comparison")
bootstrap_table.round(3)
Out[75]:
median (MW) 95% low 95% high conclusion
comparison
RMSE KNN - RMSE SVR -0.166 -0.278 -0.035 KNN better
RMSE KNN - RMSE MLP -0.214 -0.318 -0.090 KNN better
RMSE MLP - RMSE SVR 0.047 -0.013 0.106 no clear difference

KNN's advantage over both SVR and MLP is statistically clear: the intervals lie entirely below zero. SVR and MLP cannot be separated. The size of the gap still matters: about 0.2 MW of RMSE is about 0.04% of the mean output, small next to the 2.5 MW typical error of every model. KNN is measurably better on hours like those in the dataset, but not by an amount that changes an operating decision on its own.

All three models share the same pattern. Errors are smallest in the well-populated middle bands and largest at the extremes. At the low end the models over-predict, and at the high end they under-predict: predictions are pulled towards the middle where training data is dense. For operations this means the models are slightly optimistic on the worst (hottest) hours, which is the direction that risks over-committing output to the grid. Section 12 returns to this.

KNN has the smallest errors in both extreme bands, and the smallest bias at the low-output end. The MLP has the largest: in the hottest, lowest-output hours it over-predicts by about 5 MW on average.

Over-predictions by more than 5 MW are the costly error for grid commitment. KNN makes them on the fewest hours (about 5%), against about 7% for SVR and nearly 8% for the MLP. The worst single errors are similar for all three: they are the same few hours where the plant underperformed for reasons outside the data (section 7.5).

10.5 Robustness to sensor noise¶

The test inputs are exact copies of logged values. In operation, sensors drift and readings are noisy, and for day-ahead use AT, AP and RH come from a weather forecast with its own error. To test robustness, random Gaussian noise is added to the test inputs and the unchanged models are evaluated again. The reference noise level (×1) is 0.5 °C on AT, 1 cm Hg on V, 1 mbar on AP and 2 percentage points on RH; ×2 and ×3 double and triple it.

In [78]:
NOISE_SD = pd.Series({"AT": 0.5, "V": 1.0, "AP": 1.0, "RH": 2.0})
noise_rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)
base_noise = noise_rng.normal(size=X_test.shape)          # same noise draw for every model and level

noise_rows = []
for level in [0, 1, 2, 3]:
    X_noisy = X_test + base_noise * NOISE_SD.to_numpy() * level
    X_noisy["RH"] = X_noisy["RH"].clip(upper=100)
    row = {"noise level": f"x{level}"}
    for name in MODEL_ORDER:
        row[name] = root_mean_squared_error(y_test, best_models[name].predict(X_noisy))
    noise_rows.append(row)
noise_table = pd.DataFrame(noise_rows).set_index("noise level")
display(noise_table.round(3))

With clean inputs KNN leads. At realistic noise (×1), the three models are practically level (within 0.1 MW), and at higher noise the MLP degrades least while the SVR degrades most. KNN's advantage comes from matching new hours to very similar logged hours; when the inputs are noisy, the "nearest" logged hours are no longer the most similar in reality, and that advantage disappears. The MLP has learned a smooth function, so small input errors cause small output errors.

10.6 Behaviour outside the training range¶

The hottest hour in the data is 37.1 °C. A heatwave can exceed this, and these are exactly the hours when available capacity is lowest and an accurate forecast matters most. The models are asked to predict output for AT from well below to well above the observed range. The other inputs are held at the mean values of the coldest 5% of hours (cold side) and the hottest 5% (hot side), so each test point is a realistic combination.

In [79]:

SVR KNN MLP
AT (°C), hot side
37.0 436.6 430.5 431.5
40.0 446.6 430.5 428.3
42.5 452.8 430.5 424.0
45.0 455.3 430.5 419.3

Physics says output should keep falling as the air gets hotter and keep rising as it gets colder (section 2.2). The three models behave very differently once they leave the data:

  • SVR gets the direction wrong on both sides. Above about 35 °C its prediction turns upwards, reaching about 455 MW at 45 °C, roughly what the plant produces on a mild day. Below about 3 °C it turns downwards. This is a property of the RBF kernel: far from all training points the kernel terms fade out and the prediction drifts back towards the average output. In a heatwave, the SVR would tell the operator to promise far more power than the plant can deliver.
  • KNN stays flat. Outside the data, the nearest neighbours are always the most extreme logged hours, so KNN repeats their output (about 430 MW on the hot side). It cannot be badly wrong in direction, but it does not follow the further loss of output as temperature rises, so it slightly over-predicts in a heatwave.
  • The MLP follows the physical direction on both sides: output keeps falling with heat (about -1.5 MW per °C beyond 37 °C) and rising with cold. On the cold side, however, it predicts more than 500 MW, above anything the plant has ever produced, and the real plant may be limited by equipment ratings in very cold weather. Its trend is plausible, but its numbers outside the data are unverified.

The conclusion is that no model should be trusted outside the conditions it was trained on. Whatever model is chosen, it needs an operating-envelope check that flags hours whose inputs lie outside the training range.

10.7 Day-ahead model without V¶

Section 2.4 noted that for a day-ahead commitment, AT, AP and RH can come from a weather forecast, but V is a plant-side measurement that is not known in advance. Each model is refitted on AT, AP and RH only, with the hyperparameters found in sections 7 to 9, and tested.

Without V the error rises by roughly 0.6 to 0.85 MW, but every model still meets the 1% MAPE target and still beats the reference study. A day-ahead commitment based only on the weather forecast is therefore feasible. The extra error is the part of the condenser's behaviour that the weather does not determine, such as cooling-water conditions and condenser cleanliness. In practice the plant can use the three-input model for the day-ahead commitment and the four-input model for live performance monitoring.

10.8 Cost and practicality¶

In [81]:

        "saved model size (KB)": len(pickle.dumps(best_models[name])) / 1024,

Out[81]:
fit time on training set (s) prediction time per 1,000 hours (ms) saved model size (KB) needs training data at prediction time
SVR 3.365 392.025 171.699 no
KNN 0.016 10.793 382.711 yes
MLP 25.831 7.213 609.604 no

All three are cheap enough for hourly use: even the slowest, SVR, needs well under a second for 1,000 hours. KNN "trains" instantly because it only stores the training hours, but it must carry them and search them for every prediction, so its size and prediction time grow as data is added. SVR stores its support vectors (about half the training hours). The MLP's learned weights are about 25,000 numbers (about 200 KB); the saved file is larger because scikit-learn also keeps the optimizer state, but its size and prediction time stay fixed however much data it was trained on.

10.9 Final selection¶
