Selected model: KNN regression (k = 6, distance-weighted, Manhattan distance), used together with an operating-envelope check.

The reasons, in order of weight for the two uses defined in section 2.4:

  1. It makes the fewest costly errors. For grid commitment, over-prediction is the expensive mistake. KNN over-predicts by more than 5 MW on the fewest hours, and it has the smallest bias in the hottest, lowest-output hours, which are the hours where capacity is tight.
  2. It is the most accurate, and the lead is real. Its test RMSE is lower than both other models, and the bootstrap in 10.3 shows the difference is not chance. The lead is small (about 0.2 MW), so it supports the choice but would not decide it alone.
  3. Its predictions can be explained to plant staff. Each prediction is a weighted average of six real past hours with similar conditions, and those hours can be listed. This suits the condition-monitoring use: when the measured output falls short, an engineer can see which past hours the plant is being compared with.
  4. It updates instantly. New operating hours can be added without retraining, so the model's coverage grows as the plant logs more data, including hotter or colder hours than any seen so far.

Its two weaknesses are handled, not ignored:

  • It cannot extrapolate (10.6). No model here can be trusted outside the training data, and SVR is actively misleading there. The deployed model therefore includes an envelope check: an hour whose inputs fall outside the range of the training data is flagged, and its prediction is reported as uncertain. Section 11 demonstrates this.
  • Its advantage disappears when the inputs are noisy (10.5). At realistic sensor noise it is level with the other two, not worse, so this costs nothing compared with the alternatives. It is a reason to keep the plant's ambient sensors calibrated.

The MLP is the runner-up. It is the most robust to noisy inputs and the only model whose trend beyond the data follows physics, so it is the better choice if the model has to run on poor-quality inputs. It is also the reference to check KNN against when the envelope check is triggered. SVR is not recommended for deployment: it is accurate inside the data, but its behaviour in a heatwave is physically wrong in exactly the conditions where a wrong forecast costs most.

In [83]:
FINAL_MODEL_NAME = "KNN"
final_model = best_models[FINAL_MODEL_NAME]

# operating envelope: the range of each input in the training data
ENVELOPE = pd.DataFrame({"min": X_train.min(), "max": X_train.max()})


def outside_envelope(X_new):
    # names of the inputs that lie outside the training range, for each row
    low = X_new[FEATURES] < ENVELOPE["min"]
    high = X_new[FEATURES] > ENVELOPE["max"]
    return (low | high).apply(lambda r: ", ".join(r.index[r]) if r.any() else "", axis=1)


print(f"Final model: {FINAL_MODEL_NAME}")
print(f"Test RMSE {test_table.loc[FINAL_MODEL_NAME, 'test RMSE']:.2f} MW, "
      f"MAE {test_table.loc[FINAL_MODEL_NAME, 'test MAE']:.2f} MW, "
      f"MAPE {test_table.loc[FINAL_MODEL_NAME, 'test MAPE %']:.3f} %, "
      f"R² {test_table.loc[FINAL_MODEL_NAME, 'test R2']:.4f}")
print("\nOperating envelope (training range):")
display(ENVELOPE.round(2))
print(f"Test hours outside the envelope: {(outside_envelope(X_test) != '').sum()}")

test_out = X_test.join(y_test).assign(**{f"pred_{m}": test_pred[m].round(2) for m in MODEL_ORDER})
test_out.index.name = "raw_index"
test_out.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "test_predictions.csv")
print("Saved test_predictions.csv")

11. Final model on unseen input cases¶

The final model is demonstrated here on five previously unseen input cases. They are new operating conditions written for this demonstration, not rows from the dataset (the code confirms this). Each is chosen to test something specific:

  1. Hot summer afternoon: low capacity, high condenser back pressure.
  2. Cold winter night: high capacity.
  3. and 4. A mild day, once humid and once dry, with everything else identical. This isolates the humidity effect found in section 5.7.
  4. Heatwave beyond the data: AT above the hottest hour ever logged. The envelope check should flag it.

For each case the notebook reports the KNN prediction, an error band, the other two models' predictions for comparison, and whether the inputs are inside the operating envelope.

In [84]:

        {"case": "4 mild day, dry", "AT": 20.0, "V": 52.0, "AP": 1013.0, "RH": 45.0},

11.1 Predictions with an error band¶

A single number hides how far the true output could be from the prediction. The band used here comes from the final model's errors on the test set: 90% of test hours had an error between the 5th and 95th percentiles of that distribution. This is an empirical band, valid for hours like those in the dataset. It does not apply to case 5, which lies outside the data.

Each case also gets two reliability checks:

  • Range check (section 10.9): is every input inside the range seen in training?
  • Density check: KNN measures how far a new hour is from its six nearest logged hours. An hour can have every input inside its range and still be an unusual combination, for example a dry day at a temperature where dry days are rare. If the mean distance to the neighbours is larger than for 95% of test hours, the case is marked "few similar past hours".
In [85]:
final_err = test_pred[FINAL_MODEL_NAME] - y_test           # predicted - actual
q05, q95 = final_err.quantile([0.05, 0.95])
print(f"90% of test hours: actual output between prediction - {q95:.1f} MW and prediction + {-q05:.1f} MW")

scaler = final_model.named_steps["scale"]
knn = final_model.named_steps["model"]
test_dist, _ = knn.kneighbors(scaler.transform(X_test))
DENSITY_LIMIT = np.percentile(test_dist.mean(axis=1), 95)
dist, idx = knn.kneighbors(scaler.transform(cases[FEATURES]))
print(f"Density limit (95th percentile of test-hour neighbour distance): {DENSITY_LIMIT:.3f} scaled units")

results = cases.copy()
results["KNN prediction (MW)"] = final_model.predict(cases[FEATURES])
results["90% band low"] = results["KNN prediction (MW)"] - q95
results["90% band high"] = results["KNN prediction (MW)"] - q05
results["SVR (MW)"] = best_models["SVR"].predict(cases[FEATURES])
results["MLP (MW)"] = best_models["MLP"].predict(cases[FEATURES])
results["outside envelope"] = outside_envelope(cases)
results["neighbour distance"] = dist.mean(axis=1)
results["status"] = np.select(
    [results["outside envelope"] != "", results["neighbour distance"] > DENSITY_LIMIT],
    ["FLAGGED: outside training range, prediction not reliable", "caution: few similar past hours"],
    default="valid",
)
with pd.option_context("display.max_colwidth", None):
    display(results.round(1))
results.round(2).to_csv(OUT_DIR / "unseen_cases.csv")

11.3 Plausibility check¶

Each prediction is checked against the physics of section 2 and the data of section 5.

In [87]:
pred = results["KNN prediction (MW)"]

hot_band = clean[(clean["AT"].between(31, 35)) & (clean["V"].between(68, 74))][TARGET]
cold_band = clean[(clean["AT"].between(4, 8)) & (clean["V"].between(38, 42))][TARGET]

Cases 1 and 2 behave as expected:

  • The hot summer afternoon is predicted at about 434 MW, with a 90% band of roughly 429 to 439 MW. Its six neighbours are logged hours within about 1 °C, 1 cm Hg, 1 mbar and 3% RH of the case, which is closer than for a typical test hour, and their outputs range from 427 to 438 MW. All three models agree within about 1 MW.
  • The cold winter night is predicted at about 488 MW, 54 MW more than the hot afternoon, which matches the size of the seasonal swing found in section 5.7. All three models again agree within about 1.5 MW.

Cases 3 and 4 expose a real limitation of KNN. The data analysis in section 5 says the dry day should produce more power than the humid day (in the data, about 5 MW more over this RH range at a fixed temperature). KNN predicts the two almost equal, with the humid day 0.7 MW higher. The reason is in the neighbour tables. The humid case has close neighbours, all within about 1 °C of 20 °C. The dry case is an unusual combination: dry hours at 20 °C are rare, so four of its six neighbours are hours at 22.7 to 23.8 °C, and the extra warmth of those hours costs more output than the humidity gains. KNN gives every scaled input the same weight in the distance, so it cannot keep temperature fixed while it looks for neighbours. The MLP, which learned a smooth function, gets the direction right (about 3.5 MW in favour of the dry day), as does the SVR with a smaller difference.

Two things follow:

  • The two KNN predictions are still inside each other's error band, so for a single forecast the practical error is small. But KNN should not be used to read off the effect of changing one input while holding the others fixed. Section 12 therefore uses the MLP alongside KNN when it interprets feature effects.
  • The density check catches this case. The dry day is marked "few similar past hours", because its mean neighbour distance is above the limit. This is the warning an operator would see.

Case 5, the heatwave at 41 °C, is flagged by the range check. KNN repeats the output of the hottest logged hours (about 429 MW) and the MLP gives a similar 430 MW. The SVR predicts about 449 MW, more than for the 33 °C afternoon, which is physically impossible (section 10.6). Without the flag, an operator could take the SVR number at face value and promise about 15 to 20 MW more than the plant can deliver on the hottest day of the year.

11.4 Condition-monitoring demonstration¶

The second use from section 2.4 is checking plant health: comparing the measured output with what the model expects for the current conditions. The alarm threshold is set from the test errors: on 95% of normal test hours the plant produced no more than about 5 MW below the prediction. A shortfall larger than that is unusual enough to investigate.

Two readings are checked for the cold winter night (case 2): one where the plant performs normally, and one where it produces 15 MW less, as a fouled compressor or a condenser problem might cause.

In [88]:
ALARM_MW = final_err.quantile(0.95)          # shortfall exceeded on only 5% of normal test hours
expected = results.loc["2 cold winter night", "KNN prediction (MW)"]

readings = pd.DataFrame({"measured PE (MW)": [expected - 2.0, expected - 15.0]},
                        index=["normal hour", "degraded hour"])
readings["expected PE (MW)"] = expected
readings["shortfall (MW)"] = readings["expected PE (MW)"] - readings["measured PE (MW)"]
readings["alarm"] = np.where(readings["shortfall (MW)"] > ALARM_MW,
                             f"YES: shortfall above {ALARM_MW:.1f} MW, investigate", "no")
with pd.option_context("display.max_colwidth", None):
    display(readings.round(1))
measured PE (MW) expected PE (MW) shortfall (MW) alarm
normal hour 485.9 487.9 2.0 no
degraded hour 472.9 487.9 15.0 YES: shortfall above 5.2 MW, investigate

In operation, a single hour above the threshold would be noted, and a run of consecutive hours would raise an alarm. The 19 large over-predictions found in section 7.5 are real examples of the alarm case: hours in which the plant produced 24 to 48 MW less than the weather allowed.

12. Engineering interpretation¶

This section asks what the models have learned and whether it makes engineering sense, then turns the results into practical consequences and recommendations. Section 11 showed that KNN cannot isolate the effect of one input while the others stay fixed, so the feature effects here are read from the MLP, which learned a smooth function, with KNN shown alongside for comparison. Predictions themselves still come from the selected KNN model.

12.1 Which inputs matter: permutation importance¶

Permutation importance shuffles one input across the test hours, which breaks its link with the output, and measures how much the test RMSE rises. A large rise means the model depends heavily on that input. It is computed on the test set, 10 shuffles per input.

One caution: AT and V are correlated (section 3.9). Shuffling one of them creates some combinations that never occur in reality (for example a hot day with a cold condenser), which can overstate the importance of both.

In [89]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

INTERPRET = ["KNN", "MLP"]
imp_rows = []
for name in INTERPRET:
    r = permutation_importance(best_models[name], X_test, y_test, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                               n_repeats=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1)
    for f, m, s in zip(FEATURES, r.importances_mean, r.importances_std):
        imp_rows.append({"model": name, "input": f, "RMSE increase (MW)": m, "std": s})
importance = pd.DataFrame(imp_rows)

Both models give the same picture: AT far ahead, then V, with AP and RH small. This matches the physics in section 2.2 and the drop-one test in section 8.4. KNN leans more on V than the MLP does, because in KNN's distance V counts as much as AT, while the MLP has learned how much each input matters.

12.2 How each input changes the output: accumulated local effects¶

The next question is the shape of each effect: how much does output change as one input moves, with the others held at realistic values? The usual tool, the partial dependence plot, sets one input to a value for every hour in the data. With correlated inputs this creates unrealistic hours, such as 35 °C with V = 40.

Accumulated local effects (ALE) avoid this. The input's range is cut into 20 bins of equal data count. For the hours inside each bin, the model's prediction is compared with the input moved to the bin's upper edge and to its lower edge, all else unchanged. These local differences are only ever computed for hours that really have that input value, so no unrealistic combinations are used. The differences are added up across the bins and centred on zero. The resulting curve shows, in MW, how output changes along the input's range.

In [90]:
def ale_1d(model, X, feature, n_bins=20):
    # first-order accumulated local effect of one input, centred on zero
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(X[feature], np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)))
    b = np.clip(np.digitize(X[feature], edges[1:-1], right=True), 0, len(edges) - 2)
    lo, hi = X.copy(), X.copy()
    lo[feature] = edges[b]
    hi[feature] = edges[b + 1]
    local = pd.Series(model.predict(hi) - model.predict(lo)).groupby(b).mean()
    local = local.reindex(range(len(edges) - 1), fill_value=0.0)
    acc = np.concatenate([[0.0], local.cumsum().to_numpy()])
    counts = np.bincount(b, minlength=len(edges) - 1)
    centre = np.sum((acc[:-1] + acc[1:]) / 2 * counts) / counts.sum()
    return edges, acc - centre


ale = {(name, f): ale_1d(best_models[name], X_train, f) for name in INTERPRET for f in FEATURES}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.8))
for ax, f in zip(axes, FEATURES):
    for name in INTERPRET:
        edges, effect = ale[(name, f)]
        ax.plot(edges, effect, color=MODEL_COLORS[name], lw=2, label=name)
    ax.axhline(0, color=C_REF, lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set(xlabel=LABELS[f], title=f"{f}")
    ax.set_ylabel("Effect on PE (MW)" if f == "AT" else "")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
fig.suptitle("Accumulated local effect of each input on predicted output", fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig22_ale_effects.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

ale_range = pd.DataFrame({name: {f: ale[(name, f)][1].max() - ale[(name, f)][1].min() for f in FEATURES}
                          for name in INTERPRET})
ale_range.columns = [f"{c}: effect range (MW)" for c in ale_range.columns]
ale_range.round(1)

KNN: effect range (MW) MLP: effect range (MW)
AT 21.1 53.9
V 6.4 10.2
AP 3.1 3.3
RH 1.8 6.9

The MLP's effects match the physics and the data analysis on every input:

  • AT: output falls steadily with temperature, by about 54 MW across the observed range. That agrees with the 52 MW gap between the coldest and hottest hours (section 5.7). The curve is steepest between about 10 and 25 °C and flattens above 25 °C, the same convex shape seen at the hot end in section 5.2.
  • V: output falls by about 10 MW across the range of V, almost all of it between about 42 and 72 cm Hg. Higher back pressure means less steam turbine work. Above about 72 the curve turns slightly upwards; few hours lie there and they are all hot hours, so this end of the curve is poorly supported by data and should not be read as a real gain.
  • RH: output falls by about 7 MW from the driest to the most humid hours, in line with the 8 MW found in section 5.5. The model confirms the sign reversal of section 5.3: at fixed conditions, humid air lowers output.
  • AP: a small effect of about 3 MW that rises over the middle of the range and falls back at the highest pressures. Section 5.5 found the same weak, non-monotonic pattern. The model has learned that pressure matters little here, which matches the data even though ideal-gas reasoning alone would suggest a stronger effect.

KNN's curves have the same directions but are much flatter, especially for AT (about 21 MW instead of 54). Moving one input a small step rarely changes which six hours are nearest, so KNN responds to that input in coarse steps and understates its local effect. This is the same limitation found in section 11. It does not affect KNN's accuracy on real hours, where all inputs move together, but it is why the MLP is used to read the effects.

12.3 The temperature-condenser interaction¶

Section 5.4 found that V matters mainly in warm weather. If the MLP has learned this, its sensitivity to V should depend on AT. For the real training hours in each temperature band, V is raised by 1 cm Hg and the change in predicted output is averaged. This uses only realistic hours, so the result is not distorted by impossible combinations.

In [92]:

    row = {"AT band (°C)": f"{lo_}-{hi_}", "hours": len(sub), "spread of V (std)": sub["V"].std()}
    for name in INTERPRET:
        row[f"{name}: dPE/dV (MW per cm Hg)"] = (best_models[name].predict(bumped) - best_models[name].predict(sub)).mean()

The MLP's sensitivity to V is largest between 15 and 20 °C, smaller but still clear from 10 to 30 °C, and close to zero below 10 °C and above 30 °C. In the coldest and hottest bands V hardly varies (section 5.4: it sits near 40 in the cold and near 70 in the heat), so there is little for the model to learn there, and the small positive values in those bands are within noise. The model has learned the interaction found in the data: the condenser costs output mainly in the transitional and warm seasons. At about 0.2 to 0.4 MW per cm Hg, a condenser running 10 cm Hg worse than normal in spring would cost roughly 2 to 4 MW.

12.4 Causes of prediction error¶

The test RMSE of about 3.5 MW has several identifiable sources:

  1. Plant states not in the data. The largest errors (24 to 48 MW, section 7.5) are hours where the plant produced far less than the weather allowed. All three models fail on the same hours, so the cause lies outside the four inputs: a partial trip, a unit below full load for part of the hour, or a disturbance. These hours are rare but dominate the worst-case error.
  2. Sparse operating conditions. Errors are largest in the extreme output bands (section 10.4), where there are fewest training hours, and predictions there are pulled towards the middle of the range. The density check in section 11 flags such hours.
  3. Hourly averaging. Each record is an average over an hour. Two hours with the same average conditions can contain different short-term variations and so produce slightly different outputs. This sets a floor on the error that no model of hourly averages can remove.
  4. Measurement quality. V is recorded at a coarse resolution (634 distinct values) and in an unclear unit (section 3.6), and RH exceeds its physical limit in some hours (section 3.5). Section 10.5 showed that realistic sensor noise alone adds about 0.3 to 0.6 MW to the RMSE.
  5. Plant condition over time. The data spans six years, but has no timestamps or maintenance records. Compressor fouling, washing and overhauls change the output for the same weather, and the models cannot see them. They appear as unexplained scatter.

12.5 Consequences of wrong predictions, and a safety margin for grid commitment¶

If the plant commits exactly the predicted output, it will fall short on about half of all hours, because the errors are centred on zero. A shortfall has to be covered by the grid and is usually penalized; committing less than the plant can produce leaves energy unsold. Subtracting a safety margin from the prediction trades one against the other. The trade-off is computed below from the KNN test errors, scaled to a year of continuous full-load operation (8,760 hours).

In [93]:
HOURS_PER_YEAR = 8760
annual_energy = clean[TARGET].mean() * HOURS_PER_YEAR      # MWh at the average full-load output

margins = np.arange(0, 10.1, 0.5)
margin_rows = []
pred_final = test_pred[FINAL_MODEL_NAME]
for m in margins:
    committed = pred_final - m
    short = (committed - y_test).clip(lower=0)              # MW the plant fails to deliver
    unsold = (y_test - committed).clip(lower=0)             # MW the plant could have sold
    margin_rows.append({"margin (MW)": m, "hours short (%)": 100 * (short > 0).mean(),
                        "shortfall (MWh/year)": short.mean() * HOURS_PER_YEAR,
                        "unsold (MWh/year)": unsold.mean() * HOURS_PER_YEAR})
margin_table = pd.DataFrame(margin_rows)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
axes[0].plot(margin_table["margin (MW)"], margin_table["hours short (%)"], color=C_MAIN, lw=2, marker="o", markersize=4)
axes[0].set(xlabel="Safety margin below the prediction (MW)", ylabel="Hours with a shortfall (%)",
            title="Risk of not delivering the committed output")
axes[1].plot(margin_table["margin (MW)"], margin_table["shortfall (MWh/year)"] / 1000, color=C_FLAG, lw=2,
             label="shortfall (must be covered by the grid)")
axes[1].plot(margin_table["margin (MW)"], margin_table["unsold (MWh/year)"] / 1000, color=C_MAIN, lw=2,
             label="unsold (capacity not offered)")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Safety margin below the prediction (MW)", ylabel="Energy per year (GWh)",
            title="What the margin trades off")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig24_commitment_margin.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

print(f"Annual energy at average full-load output: {annual_energy / 1e6:.2f} TWh")

The best margin depends on prices that differ between markets, which this dataset does not contain. The structure of the decision is general, though. If each MWh of shortfall costs $c_s$ (the penalty) and each MWh left unsold costs $c_u$ (the lost sale), the expected cost is lowest when the margin is the quantile of the prediction error (predicted minus actual) at level $c_s / (c_s + c_u)$. This is the classical newsvendor result from operations research. The table applies it to the KNN test errors for four penalty ratios.

In [94]:
newsvendor = pd.DataFrame([
    {"penalty / sale price": r, "quantile level": r / (1 + r),
     "optimal margin (MW)": final_err.quantile(r / (1 + r)),
     "hours short (%)": 100 * (1 - r / (1 + r))}
    for r in [1, 2, 4, 9]
])
newsvendor.round(2)
Out[94]:
penalty / sale price quantile level optimal margin (MW) hours short (%)
0 1 0.50 -0.03 50.00
1 2 0.67 1.15 33.33
2 4 0.80 2.41 20.00
3 9 0.90 3.79 10.00

With equal penalty and price the best margin is about zero. With a shortfall penalty four times the sale price, the plant should commit about 2 to 3 MW below the prediction and accept a shortfall on about one hour in five. At nine times, the margin grows to about 4 MW. Because the margin comes from the error distribution, a more accurate model allows a smaller margin. That turns accuracy into money: every MW the model's error band shrinks is a MW that can be sold with the same risk.

12.6 Limitations¶

  • One plant, one operating mode. The models describe this plant at full load. They do not transfer to another plant, or to part-load operation, without new data.
  • No time information. Without timestamps the data cannot be split chronologically, and degradation or drift over the six years cannot be detected or modelled. A random split may make the test score slightly optimistic if neighbouring hours are similar.
  • Unrecorded plant events. Trips, partial outages and maintenance are not marked, so the largest errors cannot be explained or prevented with these inputs.
  • Measurement issues. The unit of V is inconsistent with its label, and RH exceeds 100% in some hours. The models are unaffected (section 3.6), but V cannot be interpreted as a true pressure.
  • Range of validity. All models are unreliable outside the observed conditions (section 10.6). The envelope and density checks flag such hours but cannot correct them.
  • KNN's equal weighting. The selected model gives every scaled input the same weight, so it cannot isolate single-input effects (section 11). For that purpose the MLP is used.

12.7 Recommendations¶

  1. Deploy the KNN model with both reliability checks. Use it hourly for performance monitoring: alarm when the measured output stays more than about 5 MW below the prediction for several consecutive hours. Show the six reference hours with each alarm so engineers can see what "normal" looked like.
  2. Commit to the grid with a margin, not the bare prediction. Choose the margin from the error distribution and the actual penalty ratio (12.5), and recompute it when the model is retrained.
  3. Use the three-input model (AT, AP, RH) for day-ahead commitments, since V is not known in advance (section 10.7). It costs under 1 MW of RMSE.
  4. Time condenser maintenance before the warm season. The condenser penalty is largest between about 15 and 30 °C (12.3 and section 5.4), so cleaning and cooling-system checks pay off most in spring.
  5. Evaluate inlet-air cooling with care. Temperature is the dominant loss (about 1.5 to 2 MW per °C), so cooling the compressor inlet on hot afternoons is the largest available lever. Evaporative coolers also raise humidity, and the models show humid air lowers output (12.2), so part of the gain is given back. The models can estimate the net effect for a proposed cooler, within the observed range of conditions.
  6. Fix the data at the source. Calibrate the RH sensor, confirm the unit and measuring point of V, record timestamps, and log trips, part-load hours and maintenance. With timestamps, the model can be validated chronologically and used to track degradation over time.
  7. Retrain regularly and watch the residuals. A steady drift of measured output below prediction over weeks is a sign of gradual fouling, which is exactly the condition-monitoring signal the plant needs.

13. Exports for the Tableau dashboard¶

The interactive dashboard is built in Tableau Public from the CSV files written here. Every number in the dashboard therefore comes from this notebook. Column names are written out in full so they can be used as chart labels directly.

Files (all in outputs/tableau/):

  1. plant_hours.csv: one row per cleaned hour, with the inputs, the actual output, the KNN prediction and its error, and grouping columns for filters.
  2. model_metrics.csv: cross-validated and test metrics of every model, in long format.
  3. error_by_band.csv: test error of each model in each 10 MW output band.
  4. feature_effects.csv: the accumulated local effect curves from section 12.2.
  5. feature_importance.csv: the permutation importances from section 12.1.
  6. unseen_cases.csv: the five cases from section 11.
  7. commitment_margin.csv: the safety-margin trade-off from section 12.5.

For training hours the prediction is the out-of-fold prediction (section 8.5), and for test hours it is the test prediction (section 10.1). Neither kind was made by a model that had seen that hour, so every error shown in the dashboard is an honest one.

TAB_DIR = OUT_DIR / "tableau"
TAB_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

NAMES = {"AT": "Ambient temperature (C)", "V": "Exhaust vacuum (cm Hg)", "AP": "Ambient pressure (mbar)",
         "RH": "Relative humidity (%)", "PE": "Net output (MW)"}

hours = clean.copy()
hours.index.name = "Hour ID"
hours["Data set"] = np.where(hours.index.isin(X_test.index), "test", "train")
hours["Prediction (MW)"] = pd.concat([oof_predictions[FINAL_MODEL_NAME], test_pred[FINAL_MODEL_NAME]]).loc[hours.index]
hours["Prediction type"] = np.where(hours["Data set"] == "test", "test prediction", "out-of-fold prediction")
hours["Error (MW)"] = hours["Prediction (MW)"] - hours[TARGET]                  # + = over-prediction
hours["Absolute error (MW)"] = hours["Error (MW)"].abs()
hours["Shortfall vs prediction (MW)"] = hours["Error (MW)"].clip(lower=0)
hours["Alarm"] = np.where(hours["Error (MW)"] > ALARM_MW, "alarm", "normal")
hours["Condenser regime"] = np.where(hours["V"] < V_SPLIT, "low V (cool season)", "high V (warm season)")
hours["Temperature band"] = pd.cut(hours["AT"], [0, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40],
                                   labels=["0-10 C", "10-15 C", "15-20 C", "20-25 C", "25-30 C", "30-40 C"]).astype(str)
hours["Output band"] = pd.cut(hours[TARGET], np.arange(420, 501, 10),
                              labels=[f"{a}-{a + 10} MW" for a in range(420, 500, 10)]).astype(str)
hours["Air density (kg/m3)"] = add_air_density(hours[FEATURES])["RHO"]
hours["Outside envelope"] = np.where(outside_envelope(hours[FEATURES]) != "", "yes", "no")

hours = hours.rename(columns=NAMES).round(3)
hours.to_csv(TAB_DIR / "plant_hours.csv")
print(f"plant_hours.csv: {len(hours):,} rows, {hours.shape[1] + 1} columns")

metric_rows = []
for name in MODEL_ORDER:
    cvt = cv_tables[name].iloc[0]
    for metric, cv_col in [("RMSE (MW)", "CV RMSE"), ("MAE (MW)", "CV MAE"), ("MAPE (%)", "CV MAPE"), ("R2", "CV R2")]:
        metric_rows.append({"Model": name, "Metric": metric, "Evaluation": "cross-validation", "Value": cvt[cv_col]})
    for metric, t_col in [("RMSE (MW)", "test RMSE"), ("MAE (MW)", "test MAE"), ("MAPE (%)", "test MAPE %"), ("R2", "test R2")]:
        metric_rows.append({"Model": name, "Metric": metric, "Evaluation": "test", "Value": test_table.loc[name, t_col]})
    metric_rows.append({"Model": name, "Metric": "Fit time (s)", "Evaluation": "cross-validation",
                        "Value": cvt["fit time (s)"]})
for metric, val in [("R2", 0.912), ("MAPE (%)", 0.872)]:
    metric_rows.append({"Model": "Reference study (gradient boosting)", "Metric": metric, "Evaluation": "test", "Value": val})
metric_rows.append({"Model": "Mean baseline", "Metric": "RMSE (MW)", "Evaluation": "test",
                    "Value": test_table.loc["mean baseline", "test RMSE"]})
pd.DataFrame(metric_rows).round(4).to_csv(TAB_DIR / "model_metrics.csv", index=False)

band_export = band_table.rename(columns={"model": "Model", "PE band": "Output band", "hours": "Test hours",
                                         "MAE": "MAE (MW)", "mean error": "Mean error (MW)"})
band_export["Output band"] = band_export["Output band"].map(lambda iv: f"{int(iv.left)}-{int(iv.right)} MW")
band_export.round(3).to_csv(TAB_DIR / "error_by_band.csv", index=False)

effect_rows = []
for (name, f), (edges, effect) in ale.items():
    for v, e in zip(edges, effect):
        effect_rows.append({"Model": name, "Input": NAMES[f], "Input value": v, "Effect on output (MW)": e})
pd.DataFrame(effect_rows).round(4).to_csv(TAB_DIR / "feature_effects.csv", index=False)

importance.assign(Input=importance["input"].map(NAMES)).rename(
    columns={"model": "Model", "RMSE increase (MW)": "RMSE increase when shuffled (MW)", "std": "Std (MW)"}
)[["Model", "Input", "RMSE increase when shuffled (MW)", "Std (MW)"]].round(3).to_csv(
    TAB_DIR / "feature_importance.csv", index=False)

results.reset_index().rename(columns={"case": "Case", **NAMES}).round(2).to_csv(TAB_DIR / "unseen_cases.csv", index=False)

margin_table.rename(columns={"margin (MW)": "Safety margin (MW)", "hours short (%)": "Hours short (%)",
